extracted.intended_audience: judges, agency officials, administrative law scholars, policymakers, and practitioners working on algorithms in government
extracted.subtask_description: A framework for distinguishing when an agency's algorithmic decision-support tool should be treated as an APA 'rule' (subject to notice-and-comment and pre-implementation review) versus nonbinding 'guidance.' The paper offers a definition of discretion plus a set of heuristics drawn from Bayesian persuasion and human-computer interaction to identify features that make an algorithm practically binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of discretion (tendency to update a default option)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discretion is focused on an adjudicator’s tendency to update a default option: adjudicators expend effort to draw upon the factual record and their own judgment to change the default disposition of a case; conversely, adjudicators lack discretion when they do not affect the probability of a given outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an algorithm is so perfect as to never need human involvement, the human has less discretion. Courts should examine whether humans meaningfully change outcomes from the algorithmic default. Example discussion: immigration judges deferring 100% to a tool — does that show abdication or accurate calibration? Use this definition as the touchstone for distinguishing rules from guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appalachian Power / practically binding functional test
rubrics_metrics.description: A document is practically binding if the agency 'acts as if a document issued at headquarters is controlling in the field,' bases enforcement actions on the document's policies or interpretations, and leads citizens to 'believe' it will be enforced as written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look at real-world agency practices rather than formal labels. Apply the three-prong functional inquiry (control in the field; basis for enforcement; reasonable expectation of enforcement) when assessing whether algorithmic documents are de facto rules. (Cites Appalachian Power Co. v. EPA.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex Ante design factors (does interface map onto the ultimate decision?)
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which an algorithm’s interface maps onto the ultimate decision an adjudicator must make—if the interface gives direct recommended actions (e.g., recommended bond amount), it is more likely to induce deference and be practically binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether algorithm output is actionable with little cognitive processing (anti-pattern) versus outputs that recommend evidence, legal frameworks, or questions (best practice). Example: a display that simply says 'BAIL' is more rulelike; one that supplies relevant record excerpts is more guidance-like.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease of independent evidentiary search / availability of supporting information
rubrics_metrics.description: How easily can an adjudicator access the underlying evidence or sources that would permit an independent conclusion? Algorithms that present or link to legal references, excerpts from the record, or other contextual information reduce the cost of independent factfinding and preserve discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools that point adjudicators to sources rather than directly recommending actions are less likely to be practically binding. Courts should examine whether the interface reduces or increases the effort required to form an independent view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives and organizational costs for dissenting from recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational incentives (promotion, penalties, performance metrics) and cultural norms that reward adherence or punish dissent affect whether a recommendation functions as binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether agencies punish mistakes more harshly when decisions conform to algorithmic recommendations or whether written-reasoning burdens fall disproportionately on dissenters. Example guidance: agencies should align performance credits to favor discretion; if they do the opposite, 'recommendations' may become rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of deviation from algorithmic recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: The real-world cost (time, career risk, workload, procedural burdens) an adjudicator faces when deviating from an algorithmic recommendation—higher costs make the recommendation more practically binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate caseload pressure, required justification for deviation, and supervisory review processes. Empirical features (e.g., credits for decisions, extra paperwork for deviations) should be considered. The harder and riskier dissent is, the more rulelike the algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explainability and informativeness of algorithmic output
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the algorithm provides interpretable reasons, explanations, or informative outputs that allow adjudicators to understand and contest the recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opaque outputs that lack explanation promote automation bias and deference. Better practice: show how the algorithm processed data, disclose objectives, and provide evidence links. Consider tradeoffs: some disclosure may implicate trade secrets, but lack of explainability weighs toward treating the tool as binding and risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimization objective (what the model is trained to optimize)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the algorithm is trained to optimize legitimate statutory or policy objectives (e.g., reduce no-shows) versus organizational goals like minimizing dissent by line adjudicators or mimicking adjudicator behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithms designed to optimize extraneous objectives (e.g., lower internal dissent) may be arbitrary-and-capricious if not aligned with statutory targets. Courts should examine training labels, loss functions, and design intent to assess legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human factors: time pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of time pressure on adjudicators (e.g., heavy caseloads) that incentivizes quick acceptance of algorithmic recommendations rather than deliberative updating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High time pressure increases automation bias and reduces meaningful discretion. Courts and agencies should evaluate workload and whether implementation context amplifies deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human factors: task complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: How cognitively complex the adjudicative task is—more complexity may increase reliance on algorithmic outputs, reducing discretion if humans cannot readily critique the recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex technical or multifactor decisions may push humans to defer. Good designs mitigate this by surfacing relevant information and scaffolding critical review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human factors: confidence and social accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudicators’ confidence levels and the social/professional accountability structures (e.g., supervisory oversight, peer norms) that affect willingness to dissent; low confidence or social penalties for dissent promote deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether dissenting is socially or professionally risky. Agencies should cultivate norms that prize dissent and design policies so costs of disagreement are not higher than costs of conformity (e.g., equalizing reporting burdens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex post factors (availability of oversight, discovery, FOIA, audits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-deployment mechanisms—judicial review under the APA, FOIA, inspectors general, third-party audits, and discovery—affect whether the tool will be subject to scrutiny and thus whether agencies will design it to preserve discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider practical availability of FOIA (and its exemptions), the prospect of APA suits and discovery, and whether agency inventories (statutory reporting) exist. The ability to obtain information ex post can mitigate risks, but limitations (deliberative process exemption, resource constraints) reduce that mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood of automation bias (tendency to rubber-stamp algorithm)
rubrics_metrics.description: The propensity for human adjudicators to over-rely on algorithmic outputs—especially when outputs match priors or are presented as authoritative—reduces meaningful human decisionmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices that reduce automation bias (e.g., providing sources, requiring routine explanatory reasoning, randomized rollouts to measure discretion) help preserve discretion. Empirical evidence (e.g., Dutch Tax Authority, Dutch childcare scandal) demonstrates harms from automation bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interface granularity: recommending actions vs recommending sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the tool issues actionable recommendations (specific decisions) or merely points to sources/queries/questions; recommending sources increases cognitive work and preserves discretion, while recommending actions is more rulelike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should favor guidance-like treatment for tools that facilitate independent factfinding (e.g., citation/relevant-document recommendations). Agencies should prefer designs that increase 'cognitive frictions' between output and final decision to avoid creating de facto rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational design levers to encourage dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency procedural and cultural mechanisms (e.g., assignment of decision credits, written-reasoning requirements applied uniformly, involvement of line officers in design) that make dissent inexpensive or rewarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice includes assigning more credits to discretionary decisions, avoiding asymmetric burdens (don't require writing only when deviating), involving frontline staff in UI design, and collecting data (ideally via randomized rollouts) to verify exercise of discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and procurement transparency (procurement clauses and auditor access)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procurement and contracting provisions that require ethical AI standards, limited waivers for trade secrets, and third-party auditability increase external reviewability and transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies procuring third-party models should include contractual requirements for explainability, standards conformance, and audit access. Such measures make algorithmic systems less likely to function as opaque rules and facilitate oversight.
